opus-5.5.text:
I like to think of it as a ladder, and mathematics is a really clean place to see every rung.

At the bottom you have tasks where the answer is basically retrieval plus a bit of pattern matching: solving a textbook integral, or a competition problem whose technique has appeared a thousand times before. Models are already very good at that. A step up is where you need to chain many steps together without making a mistake. That's where things used to break, because a tiny error in step seven quietly ruins everything after it. This is a big reason I care so much about formal verification, things like Lean. If every step is checked by a machine, you stop worrying about whether the model "sounds" right and start knowing whether it *is* right.

Then there's the rung that I think people underestimate: long-horizon work. A real research problem isn't one clever trick. It's weeks of trying things, building up lemmas, abandoning approaches, and noticing that some side result is actually the interesting thing. That requires memory, planning, and a kind of taste about what's worth pursuing.

And at the very top is what I'd honestly call superhuman. It isn't solving a hard problem faster than a person. It's proposing the *right questions*: inventing a new definition or a new framework that reorganizes a field, the way Grothendieck did. I don't think we're there. But I don't think it's magic either. If you have a system that can generate conjectures, attempt proofs, and get perfectly reliable feedback from a verifier, you get a self-improving loop that humans simply can't run at that scale.

So for me the range isn't a smooth line from easy to hard. It goes from *answering*, to *reasoning reliably*, to *researching*, and eventually to *discovering*. Math happens to be the domain where each of those transitions is measurable, which is why I think it'll be one of the first places we actually see superhuman AI, not just hear about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a ladder from answering to discovering; it does not frame the progression as moving from a plate’s center to its outer rim.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as a spectrum, and the easiest way to picture it is to anchor the two ends and then ask what sits in between.

At the simple end you have tasks where a model is essentially doing pattern completion: summarizing a paper, writing boilerplate code, translating a lemma statement into Lean syntax. These are useful, but they aren't fundamentally different from what a careful undergraduate could do with enough time. The model is faster and cheaper, not smarter.

At the far end you have things no human has ever done. Proving a conjecture that has been open for fifty years. Finding a structure in a mathematical object that nobody suspected was there. Discovering a result that doesn't just answer a question but reframes what the interesting questions are. That's what I'd actually call superhuman, and I want to be strict about the word. Beating humans at speed or breadth is not superhuman in the sense that matters. Superhuman means producing knowledge that was not accessible to us before.

The interesting part is the middle, because it isn't a smooth ramp. In mathematics specifically, there's a sharp transition somewhere around the level of research problems. Competition math, even very hard competition math, has a known answer and a known shape of solution. Someone wrote the problem, so someone already understands it. Research is different. You often don't know if the statement is true. You don't know which tools apply. You might spend six months and discover you were asking the wrong question. The feedback loop goes from minutes to months, and the search space goes from large to essentially unbounded.

So when I picture the range, I don't see a ruler with evenly spaced marks. I see a long stretch of tasks that are basically solved or will be soon, then a cliff, and then a very different landscape on the other side. The models we have today are climbing the cliff. They can do pieces of research: verify proofs, explore special cases, suggest lemmas, run through enormous numbers of candidate approaches overnight. What they mostly can't do yet is sustain a direction over a long time horizon with taste about what matters.

My personal bet is that the cliff gets climbed, and that math is one of the first places it happens, because we have formal verification. A proof in Lean is either correct or it isn't. That gives you a training signal that most fields don't have. You can let a system explore aggressively and be wrong a million times, because the checker catches every mistake. Biology doesn't have that. Economics doesn't have that. Math does, and that makes it a kind of leading indicator for what superhuman work looks like.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming that once you get one superhuman result, you've crossed over for good. I think the first superhuman results will look narrow and a bit strange. A proof nobody can read. A counterexample found by brute force that happens to settle a real question. It'll take a while before we get systems that are superhuman in the way a great mathematician is, where the achievement comes with understanding and explanation and a sense of why it was worth doing. That's the end of the range I actually care about reaching.

r001.rationale: The response describes a spectrum with a cliff between ordinary tasks and research, but it does not frame the progression as movement from a plate’s center to its outer rim.

astra-6.text:
I picture it as a spectrum, but probably not a single straight line. At one end, you have tasks where success is easy to check—sorting information, transcribing audio, or following a clear set of instructions. Then you move toward tasks that require more judgment: solving an unfamiliar problem, deciding which questions matter, or working toward a goal over many steps.

At the superhuman end, I’d imagine systems that can discover things we couldn’t discover ourselves—perhaps finding a mathematical proof or identifying a scientific pattern that’s beyond our ability to see. But a system could be superhuman in one area and still struggle with something that feels simple to us. So the interesting question is not just how high its capabilities go, but how broadly and reliably it can apply them.

r001.rationale: The response describes a spectrum from easy-to-check tasks to superhuman discoveries, but does not frame it as movement from a plate’s center to its outer rim.

sol-6.1.text:
I picture it as a spectrum. At one end, you have fairly well-defined tasks, like sorting information or summarizing a document. Then you move toward problems that require more reasoning, planning, and creativity. At the far end, you have systems that could make discoveries or solve problems beyond what any individual human can do.

But I don’t think it’s a single ladder. An AI might be superhuman in one narrow area and still struggle with something we find very simple. The interesting question is how those different capabilities come together—and whether they let us tackle problems we couldn’t solve before.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a spectrum from simple tasks to superhuman capabilities, but does not frame it as movement from the center of a plate to its outer rim.
